15. The allegation is that the accused was cheated government for not paying VAT amount to make wrongful gain for herself and thereby committed the offence punishable under section 420 of IPC.

In this context it is relevant to reiterate Section 415 of Indian Penal Code defines cheating "Whoever,
by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, or intentionally induces the person so deceived to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not so KABC030156552014 CC No.5239/2014 deceived, and which act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property, is said to "cheat".
It has been held in the case of Hridaya Ranjan Verma and others Vs State of Bihar and another reported in 2000(4) SCC 168 and in the case of Indian Oil Corporation Vs NEPC India Limited and others reported in 2006(6) SCC 736, this Court held :

entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Indian Oil Corporation Vs NEPC India Limited and others reported in 2006(6) SCC 736
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: On a reading of the section it is manifest that in the definition there are set forth two separate classes of acts which the person deceived may be induced to do.
In the first place he may be induced fraudulently or dishonestly to deliver any property to any person.
The second class of acts set forth in the section is the doing or omitting to do anything which the person deceived would not do or omit to do if he were not so deceived.
In the first class of cases the inducing must be fraudulent or dishonest.
In the second class of acts, the inducing must be intentional but not fraudulent or dishonest.

Thus, the ingredients of Section 420 of the Indian Penal Code are as follows :
(i) Deception of any persons;
(ii) Fraudulently or dishonestly inducing any person to deliver any property; or (iii) to consent that any person shall retain any property and finally intentionally inducing that person to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
In this context it is relevant to reiterate Section 415 of Indian Penal Code defines cheating "Whoever,
by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, or intentionally induces the person so deceived to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not so KABC030156552014 CC No.5239/2014 deceived, and which act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property, is said to "cheat".
It has been held in the case of Hridaya Ranjan Verma and others Vs State of Bihar and another reported in 2000(4) SCC 168 and in the case of Indian Oil Corporation Vs NEPC India Limited and others reported in 2006(6) SCC 736, this Court held :
14.
On a reading of the section it is manifest that in the definition there are set forth two separate classes of acts which the person deceived may be induced to do.
The second class of acts set forth in the section is the doing or omitting to do anything which the person deceived would not do or omit to do if he were not so deceived.
In the first class of cases the inducing must be fraudulent or dishonest.
In the second class of acts, the inducing must be intentional but not fraudulent or dishonest.
17. Apart from which, it is the case of prosecution that the accused did not run the business from July 2010 till September 2011 and raised the bills in favour of different companies and some unknown companies which are not in existence.
If such was the thing, then prosecution could have produced the same with cogent evidence apart from investigation report as per Ex.P11.
Without furnishing the audit report of the accused and without cross verification of bills submitted by the accused with the said purchasers, how this court could come to a conclusion that the accused has committed the alleged offence and the said factum was admitted by the PW1 in his cross examination, without the audit report, they cannot come to a conclusion that the accused has cheated the government.
M.Nagendra vs Saroja Agarwal on 5 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/182096509/
7 KABC030156552014 CC No.5239/2014 19.

.
Thus, it is clear that PW3 has not drawn any panchaname and more so when he had visited the said building all the shops were closed and hence such being the case, without inquiring the accused about the closure of shop on the said date of visit i.e., 03/09/2011 cannot come to a conclusion that the accused has closed down the shop.
20. Added to which, PW3 had given an inspection report that the accused proprietor concern had a bogus transaction with M/s M. N. Steel, Bangalore Enterprises, Sun Tools and Shakthi Trading company and Sun Enterprises as per Ex.P10.
21.
On what basis, PW3 had come to a conclusion that the aforesaid 8 companies were bogus dealers when PW1 and PW3 did not issue notice to the said dealers nor enquired with them and KABC030156552014 CC No.5239/2014 more so PW5 and PW7 did not ascertain about the said transaction had taken place with the said dealers or not or such dealers was in existence at that time of transaction or such dealers was not in existence at at that time of transaction and such being the case without any material to corroborate how this court could come to conclusion that the accused created the bogus dealers to evade the tax cannot be accepted.
23. It is relevant to mention section 21 and 22 of Karnataka Tax on Entry of Goods Act 1979 which reads as under 21.
Thus, the very taking cognizance of offense without previous sanction of Joint commissioner of Commercial Tax Office against the accused is contrary to section 21(2) of Karnataka Tax on Entry of M.Nagendra vs Saroja Agarwal on 5 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/182096509/
9 Goods Act 1979 and thereby the case of prosecution fails on this ground.
Therefore, the prosecution failed to prove the charges against the accused beyond all reasonable doubt thereby this court answers the above point No.1 in the negative.

24. Point No. 2:- For the foregoing discussion and the findings to the above point No.1, this court proceeds to pass the following:
KABC030156552014 CC No.5239/2014 ORDER Acting U/Sec.248(1) of the Cr.P.C.
(i) The accused is found not guilty and acquitted from the offence punishable under Sec.420 of IPC.
(ii) Accused is set at liberty.
(iii) In view of Section 437-A of Cr.P.C her bail bond shall be in force for 6 (six)
months.
